en: The entire collection of sounds, whether they convey meaning or are meaningless, is designated by the alternative name *dhvani*. As it is stated in the *Paspaśāhnika* of Patañjali’s *Mahābhāṣya*: "Alternatively, in common usage, *dhvani* is that which has its word-meaning understood."

By this, the fact that meaningful sound (*śabda*) is of the nature of resonance (*dhvani*) attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it is well known in the world that even meaningless sound is called *dhvani*. Moreover, in the science of the new *dhvani* theory, every kind of sound is termed *dhvani*. The threefold speech—namely, the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*), which is the very nature of consciousness and consists of the potency of mantra (*mantravīrya*), as well as the Visionary Speech (*paśyantī*) and the Intermediate Speech (*madhyamā*)—is also designated by the term *dhvani*. As it is said:
"Thus, that which arises in the abode of the attainment of immersion into the threefold emission (*visarga*)."
Consciousness, whose nature is reflective awareness (*parimarśa*), is *dhvani*; that alone is the potency (*vīrya*) of mantra.

Here, by the phrase "consciousness, whose nature is reflective awareness," *parāvāk* is understood. Since *paśyantī* is rooted in *parāvāk*, she too has the nature of *dhvani*. The use of the term *dhvani* for *madhyamā* speech is stated in the *Yogacūḍāmaṇi Upaniṣad*:
"Like a continuous stream of oil, like the long resonance of a bell..."
In the same way, the resonance of the Praṇava is called that [Supreme] Brahman. ||8||

Thus, since every kind of sound is conventionally designated by the synonym *nīti*—as used by the authors of the treatises—all sound whatsoever is called *dhvani*. Therefore, one should not accept the view that "only the phonemes (*varṇa*) such as 'a' and so forth are denoted by the term *dhvani*, but not the *parā* speech and the others.

Precisely because of the practice of treating the words *dhvani* and *śabda* as non-different, the established doctrine (*samaya*) of the Grammarians is that "sound (*dhvani*) alone is speech (*śabda*). And it has been said by the venerable Bhartṛhari in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* of the *Vākyapadīya*:
"Some who follow the ancient [tradition] say that there is a distinction between these two [the phoneme and the sound]."
"Some declare that because of the difference in cognition, there is a difference in what is non-different.

"Alternatively, in common usage, a sound (*dhvani*) whose object is understood is called 'word' (*śabda*). For example, one says: 'Make a sound,' 'Do not make a sound,' or 'This boy is making a sound. It is while he is actually producing a sound that he is so addressed. Therefore, sound is the word. Here, sound alone is the word; the relationship between sound and word is one of identity (*abheda*). Without sound, there is no cognition of the word as such; therefore, sound alone is the word."
